Lecture 17-1

When does a fixed bed stop being enough?

Catalyst lifeCoke as the clockPressure against lifeThree ways to regenerate

Lecture 17-1

The life of the catalyst decides how it is held in the reactor

  1. Catalyst life sets the reactor typeseconds, days or years between regenerations
  2. Coke is the clockactivity falls as coke builds on the catalyst
  3. Lower pressure: more yield, shorter lifewhat four generations of reformers traded
  4. Three ways to regenerateshut down, swing a reactor, or keep the catalyst moving

Catalyst life · try it

How long the catalyst lives decides how it must be held

–

–

Between about a day and a month the catalyst dies too fast for a shutdown and too slowly for fluidization: that is the moving bed’s window.

What sets that time in reforming is coke laid down on the catalyst.

Coke as the clock

Activity falls exponentially with the coke on the catalyst

$$a=\frac{r(C_c)}{r(C_c=0)}=e^{-\alpha C_c}$$
$a$
activity: rate now ÷ rate on fresh catalyst
–
$C_c$
coke on catalyst
kg/kg cat
$\alpha$
deactivation constant, fitted to data
kg cat/kg

Coke-based deactivation function of Froment and Bischoff; in this lecture $\alpha=13.9$, so 5 wt% coke halves activity.

  • Coke grows from olefin and aromatic precursors on metal and acid sites.
  • Hydrogen hydrogenates the precursors, so lower H2 partial pressure means faster coking.
  • Higher temperature also speeds coking.

Coke forces regeneration; the question is how to do it without losing production.

Three ways to regenerate

Shut the unit down, swing one reactor out, or never stop the catalyst

Semiregenerative (SR)

Fixed beds; the whole unit stops to burn the coke. Cycle 6–24 months.

57 % of world reforming capacity (Aitani)

Cyclic

Fixed beds plus a swing reactor; one reactor at a time is isolated and regenerated, every 3–30 days.

11 %

Continuous (moving bed)

Catalyst flows through the reactors to a separate regenerator and back: Continuous Catalyst Regeneration (CCR).

27 %, and >95 % of new units (Treese)

Each design was pushed to lower pressure; here is what that cost in catalyst life.

Pressure against life · click a generation

Each generation of reformer cut the pressure and paid with catalyst life

–

–

From 450 to 50 psig the octane rose from about 95 to 108 while regeneration went from once a year to once every few days (Treese, Lapinski et al.).

The decisive comparison

At CCR conditions a fixed bed would be dead in a few days

  • “At CCR conditions, the SR catalyst would be completely deactivated after only a few days” (Treese).
  • So the catalyst must keep moving: out of the reactors, through a regenerator, and back.

Section 17-1 · summary

The catalyst’s life, not the chemistry alone, chooses the reactor

  • Catalyst life from about a day to a month points to a moving bed.
  • $a=e^{-\alpha C_c}$: coke is the clock, and it runs faster at low H2 pressure and high temperature.
  • Low pressure raises reformate, aromatics and hydrogen yield, but shortens the cycle to days.
  • SR stops the unit, cyclic swings a reactor out, CCR keeps the catalyst moving.

Lecture 17-2

A moving bed is a packed bed that slides slowly downward

  1. Fixed, moving and fluidized bedswhat moves, how fast, and what it costs
  2. Three ways for gas to meet the solidco-current, counter-current, cross-flow
  3. How granular solids flowplug descent, opening sizes, residence time
  4. Why the catalyst is a sphererolling instead of breaking

Fixed, moving, fluidized

A moving bed keeps the packing of a fixed bed and the circulation of a fluid bed

Fixed bedMoving bedFluidized bed
Solidsat restslide down as a plug, cm/h to m/hsuspended and mixed
Void fraction $\varepsilon$≈ 0.4≈ 0.4, packed0.5–0.8
Gas flownear plug flownear plug flowbubbles, bypass
Regenerationstop or swingcontinuous, separate vesselcontinuous, separate vessel
Wear on catalystlowmoderate: lift lines, valveshigh: attrition

Henkel (Ullmann’s): moving beds allow continuous regeneration but load the catalyst and the internals mechanically.

Inside the moving bed, gas and solid can meet in three directions.

Contact patterns · click a pattern

The gas may run with, against, or across the descending catalyst

–

–

Reforming and dehydrogenation use cross-flow: a thin radial bed gives a short gas path, so a huge gas flow passes with a small pressure drop.

The catalyst is not a liquid: it flows like sand in an hourglass.

Solids flow

A granular bed descends as a plug, and its outlet must be wide

  • Outlets narrower than about 6 particle diameters block; practice is 15–20.
  • Discharge rate barely depends on bed height: the weight is carried by the walls.
  • Poured solids form a cone at the angle of repose, about 38°.

Raseev, §5.3.3, characteristics of the moving bed.

Solids flow · try it

The catalyst creeps down at centimetres per hour and stays for days

$$v_s=\frac{F_s}{\rho_b\,A},\qquad \tau_s=\frac{W}{F_s}$$
$F_s$
catalyst circulation rate
kg/h
$\rho_b$, $A$
bulk density; bed cross-section
kg/m³, m²
$W$
catalyst in all reactors
kg
$v_s$ in R4 (cm/h)–
$\tau_s$ (h)–
loop time (days)–

R4 holds 40 % of $W$ in an annulus $r_i=0.6$ m, $r_o=1.6$ m, $\rho_b=650$ kg/m³.

At 1 t/h of catalyst a 90 t inventory turns over every 3.6 days, inside the 3–7 days reported for CCR units.

Why spheres

Spheres roll through reactors, valves and lift lines without breaking

  • Catalyst rubs on screens and other pellets, falls into hoppers and passes lock-hopper valves.
  • Spheres of 1.5–1.9 mm, density 0.5–0.7 g/cm³, keep breakage low (Treese).
  • Fines are still made, so make-up catalyst is added and fines are removed.

Section 17-2 · summary

A packed bed that slides: plug flow for gas and for catalyst

  • Moving bed: packed like a fixed bed ($\varepsilon\approx0.4$), circulated like a fluid bed.
  • Gas may flow co-current, counter-current or across; reformers use cross-flow radial beds.
  • $v_s=F_s/(\rho_bA)$ is centimetres per hour; $\tau_s=W/F_s$ is days.
  • Outlets of 15–20 particle diameters and spherical catalyst keep the solids moving.

The family · click a process

Five commercial processes that keep their catalyst moving

–

All five share one idea: the catalyst life is days to weeks, so it is replaced while the unit runs.

Dehydrogenation is the second big user, with the same regenerator idea.

Dehydrogenation

Oleflex runs propane dehydrogenation in radial moving beds with a CCR

Main reaction$\mathrm{C_3H_8\;\rightleftharpoons\;C_3H_6+H_2}\qquad \Delta H>0$
  • Pt–Sn catalyst, 3–4 moving beds with interheaters; hydrogen-to-hydrocarbon ratio (H2/HC) 2–3.
  • About 40 % propane conversion per pass, near equilibrium; >86 wt% selectivity.
  • Catalyst loop: 5–10 days (Meyers, Ch. 5.1).

Reforming is the main case for the rest of the lecture, so first its chemistry.

Reforming reactions

Fast endothermic dehydrogenation first, slow paraffin reactions last

Paraffin $\to$ aromatic (dehydrocyclization)endothermicslowR2–R4
Paraffin hydrocrackingexothermicslowmostly R4
Coke formation–slowgrows with T, low H2

Pt sites dehydrogenate; chlorided alumina sites isomerize and crack (Treese, Lapinski et al.).

Section 17-3 · summary

Moving beds carry the processes whose catalyst lives days, not years

  • CCR reforming, Octanizing, Oleflex and Cyclar use radial moving beds plus a regenerator.
  • Residue bunker reactors move the catalyst to replace metal-loaded pellets.
  • Reforming: fast endothermic naphthene dehydrogenation first, slow paraffin reactions last.
  • Low pressure with CCR: more octane, more and purer hydrogen, more reformate.

Lecture 17-4

  1. The catalyst loopreactors, collector, lift lines, regenerator, reduction

The catalyst loop · click a part

Catalyst falls through the reactors, is lifted to the regenerator, and comes back new

Click a part of the loop

The catalyst never stops; the gas passes R1 to R4 with a heater before each reactor.

Reactors and regenerator can be isolated from each other, so the regenerator can stop for maintenance while naphtha keeps flowing (Treese).

Two designs

UOP stacks the reactors; Axens puts them side by side and lifts between them

UOP CCR PlatformingAxens Octanizing / Aromizing
Reactorsstacked in one columnside by side
Catalyst between reactorsfalls by gravitylifted by H2 from each reactor to the next
To and from regeneratorN2 lift linesN2 lift lines
Flow controllock hoppers and lift gascollector level and secondary H2; no valves on catalyst lines

Raseev, §13.7; Treese. Stacking removes the lifts between reactors.

Every reactor in either design has the same inside: a radial bed.

Radial-flow internals

Gas crosses a thin annulus of falling catalyst into the centre pipe

  • Gas enters through scallops or an outer basket at the wall.
  • It crosses the catalyst annulus radially, inward.
  • A profile-wire centre-pipe screen holds the catalyst and collects the gas (Treese).

Section 17-4 · summary

A CCR is two loops: gas through heaters, catalyst through a regenerator

  • Catalyst falls R1→R4, is lifted by N2 to the regenerator, then reduced and returned.
  • UOP stacks the reactors; Axens places them side by side and lifts between them.
  • Each reactor is a radial annulus: gas in at the wall, out through the centre pipe.
  • The reactions absorb heat, so four reactors with interheaters; R1 cools the most.

Lecture 17-5

The gas must pass easily, but not so hard that it holds the catalyst still

  1. Ergun in radial coordinatesvelocity changes with radius
  2. Axial against radial bedsame catalyst, pressure drop differs by a factor of 100
  3. Pinninggas drag presses the catalyst onto the centre screen

Radial Ergun

In a radial bed the gas speeds up as it moves inward

Ergun, Lecture 15$-\dfrac{dP}{dz}=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)}{Re}\Big]\dfrac{G^2}{\rho_gd_p},\quad G=\rho_gu,\quad Re=\dfrac{d_pG}{\mu}$
$u(r)=\dfrac{Q}{2\pi rH}$
same flow crosses a smaller cylinder
$-\dfrac{dP}{dr}=\text{Ergun}\big(u(r)\big)$
replace $z$ by the radial path
$\Delta P=\displaystyle\int_{r_i}^{r_o}\text{Ergun}\big(u(r)\big)\,dr$
integrate across the bed thickness
$Q$

m³/s
$r_i$, $r_o$, $H$

Example 17.1 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 17.1Why the bed must be radial

A CCR reformer processes 30,000 BPSD of naphtha (density 740 kg/m³, molar mass 110 kg/kmol) with recycle hydrogen at H2/HC = 2.5 mol/mol. The fourth reactor, R4, operates at 520 °C and 4.5 bar abs and holds 36 t of spherical catalyst ($d_p$ = 1.6 mm, bulk density 650 kg/m³, $\varepsilon$ = 0.40). The gas viscosity is 1.8 × 10−5 Pa s.

(a) Calculate the actual gas volume flow and density through R4, treating the recycle gas as pure H2.

(b) Calculate the pressure drop if the catalyst is loaded as an axial bed 3.2 m in diameter, and as a radial bed with $r_i$ = 0.6 m and $r_o$ = 1.6 m. Which design can work?

Example 17.1 · solution (a)

EXAMPLE 17.1About 19 m³ of gas crosses R4 every second

Ideal gas$Q=\dfrac{F\,RT}{P},\qquad \rho_g=\dfrac{\dot m}{Q}$
$F_{HC}=\dfrac{30\,000\times0.159\times740}{24\times110}=1337$ kmol/h
barrel = 0.159 m³
$F=1337\times(1+2.5)=4679$ kmol/h;  $\dot m=1.54\times10^5$ kg/h
naphtha plus recycle H2
$Q=\dfrac{1.300\times10^3\times8.314\times793}{4.5\times10^5}=19.0$ m³/s,  $\rho_g=2.24$ kg/m³
mol/s at 793 K, 4.5 bar

Hydrogen made in R1–R3 is ignored, so the real flow is a little higher.

Example 17.1 · solution (b)

EXAMPLE 17.1Axial: 9.9 bar, more than the inlet pressure. Radial: 0.056 bar

Ergun and radial velocity$-\dfrac{dP}{dz}=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)}{Re}\Big]\dfrac{G^2}{\rho_gd_p},\qquad u(r)=\dfrac{Q}{2\pi rH}$
Axial: $A=8.04$ m², $L=6.9$ m, $u=2.37$ m/s, $Re=472$: $\Delta P=1.43\times10^5\times6.9=9.9$ bar
impossible at 4.5 bar abs
Radial: $H=\dfrac{55.4}{\pi(1.6^2-0.6^2)}=8.0$ m; $u$ = 0.24 m/s outside, 0.63 m/s inside
bed volume 36/0.65 = 55.4 m³
$\Delta P=\int_{0.6}^{1.6}\text{Ergun}\,dr=5.6$ kPa $=0.056$ bar
numerical integration, 175 times smaller

Axial against radial · try it

A short gas path through a large area keeps the pressure drop small

bed height $H$ (m)–
radial ΔP (kPa)–
axial ΔP, D = 3.2 m (kPa)–

Same 55 m³ of catalyst and Example 17.1 gas: a thinner annulus is taller and has less pressure drop, because both path length and velocity fall.

Low pressure drop is good, but the gas also pushes on the catalyst.

Pinning

Too much gas presses the catalyst onto the centre screen and holds it there

  • Drag pushes the bed inward; the screen pushes back, and wall friction resists descent.
  • If friction exceeds the weight, catalyst at the screen stops: it is pinned, overheats and cokes.
  • Pinning is a real feed-rate constraint in advanced control of reformers (Turpin, in Antos Ch. 14).

Pinning · force balance

Compare the friction from total drag with the weight of the bed

$F_d=\displaystyle\int_{r_i}^{r_o}\Big(-\frac{dP}{dr}\Big)2\pi rH\,dr$
total drag on the annulus
$\Pi=\dfrac{\mu_w\,F_d}{\rho_b\,g\,V_{bed}}$
friction over weight
$\Pi<1$: catalyst moves;  $\Pi\ge1$: pinned
screen friction carries the whole bed
$\mu_w$
catalyst–screen friction coefficient, about 0.3 here
–
$V_{bed}$
catalyst bed volume
m³

Simplified balance built for this lecture: ignores arching and particle–particle shear; vendors use tested limits.

Capacity limit · try it

Raise the gas flow until the catalyst pins

Previous slide$\Pi=\dfrac{\mu_w F_d}{\rho_b g V_{bed}}$
ΔP (kPa)–
$\Pi$–

With $\mu_w$ = 0.3 the design bed pins at about 2.4 times its gas flow; drag grows faster than flow, as $Q^{1.6-1.7}$.

Section 17-5 · summary

Radial flow solves the pressure drop; pinning sets the ceiling

  • Ergun with $u=Q/(2\pi rH)$, integrated from $r_i$ to $r_o$, gives the radial-bed ΔP.
  • Same catalyst: about 10 bar as an axial bed, 0.06 bar as a radial bed.
  • Drag presses the bed onto the centre screen; friction can stop it (pinning).
  • $\Pi=\mu_wF_d/(\rho_bgV_{bed})$ must stay below 1: gas rate is capped.

17-6

Lecture 17-6

How are the balances written when the catalyst moves?

Age = positionCoke balanceActivity profileCross-flow mean

Lecture 17-6

Moving the catalyst turns a time problem into a steady position problem

  1. Catalyst age is positionwhy a moving bed is at steady state
  2. The coke balancecirculation rate from the coke made
  3. The activity profilefresh at the top of R1, oldest at the bottom of R4
  4. Gas across ageing catalystcross-flow outlet as a mean over the height

Age = position

Each height in the bed always holds catalyst of the same age

$$\theta=\frac{z_s}{v_s}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{\text{fixed bed}}\;\to\;v_s\frac{d}{dz_s}\Big|_{\text{moving bed}}$$
$\theta$
catalyst age since it left the regenerator
h
$z_s$
distance travelled by the catalyst
m
$v_s$
catalyst descent speed, $F_s/(\rho_bA)$
m/h
  • In a fixed bed, activity falls with time: an unsteady problem.
  • In a moving bed, it falls with position; at one height it never changes.
  • So the whole unit runs at steady state, with constant yields.

Coke balance

Coke grows along the catalyst path; the regenerator removes it all

$\dfrac{dC_c}{d\theta}=r_c$
coke laydown per kg of catalyst
$C_c(\theta)=C_{c,in}+r_c\,\theta$
$r_c$ constant at given conditions
$F_s\big(C_{c,out}-C_{c,in}\big)=r_c\,W=R_c$
over the loop, $\tau_s=W/F_s$
$r_c$
coke laydown rate per kg catalyst
kg/(kg·h)
$C_{c,in}$, $C_{c,out}$
coke entering R1, leaving R4
kg/kg cat
$R_c$
coke made by the whole unit
kg/h

Example 17.2 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 17.2Catalyst circulation from a coke balance

The CCR reformer of Example 17.1 charges 30,000 BPSD of naphtha (740 kg/m³) and lays down coke equal to 0.035 wt% of the naphtha. The reactors hold 90 t of catalyst (bulk density 650 kg/m³). Regenerated catalyst enters R1 with 0.1 wt% coke; spent catalyst must leave R4 with no more than 5.0 wt% coke (both per mass of coke-free catalyst).

(a) Find the catalyst circulation rate $F_s$. (b) How long does one pass through the reactors take? (c) What is the liquid hourly space velocity (LHSV), feed volume per hour over catalyst volume? (d) What is $r_c$?

Example 17.2 · solution

EXAMPLE 17.2About 1 t/h of catalyst; one pass every 3.6 days

Coke balance, previous slide but one$F_s\big(C_{c,out}-C_{c,in}\big)=r_cW=R_c,\qquad \tau_s=\dfrac{W}{F_s}$
$\dot m_{feed}=\dfrac{30\,000\times0.159\times740}{24}=147\,060$ kg/h;  $R_c=0.00035\,\dot m_{feed}=51.5$ kg/h
coke made per hour
(a) $F_s=\dfrac{51.5}{0.050-0.001}=1050$ kg/h   (b) $\tau_s=\dfrac{90\,000}{1050}=85.7$ h $=3.6$ d
inside the reported 3–7 days
(c) $\mathrm{LHSV}=\dfrac{198.7}{90\,000/650}=1.43$ h−1   (d) $r_c=\dfrac{51.5}{90\,000}=5.7\times10^{-4}$ h−1
LHSV typical 1–3 h−1

Raseev reports 900–1360 kg/h of regeneration for 4000 m³/day units: the same order.

R4 always holds the oldest catalyst; doubling $F_s$ halves the coke on it, at the cost of twice the regenerator load.

Within one reactor the gas also meets catalyst of different ages.

Cross-flow

Gas at each height meets one age; the outlet is a mean over the height

$X(\xi)=1-e^{-Da\,a(\xi)}$
plug flow across, first order

Section 17-6 · summary

Age becomes position, so the moving bed is a steady-state reactor

  • $\theta=z_s/v_s$: the unsteady fixed-bed problem becomes a steady one.
  • $F_s(C_{c,out}-C_{c,in})=r_cW$ sets the circulation; $\tau_s=W/F_s$ the loop time.
  • Activity falls from R1 to R4; faster circulation flattens the profile.
  • Cross-flow outlet = mean over height ≈ value at mid-height activity.

Example 17.3 · solving in EQUATRAN

EXAMPLE 17.3Four integrations in series, one per reactor

  • Compute $a_1\ldots a_4$ first: they are constants for the gas balances.
  • Integrate $N$, $P$, $T$ over $\omega$ from 0 to the reactor’s catalyst fraction; outlet $N$, $P$ feed the next reactor, $T$ restarts at 520 °C.
  • Aromatics out $=A_0+(N_0-N)+(P_0-P-\text{cracked})$; track the cracked paraffins as a fourth variable.
  • For the fixed bed, repeat with one $a$ for all reactors at each day on stream.

Section 17-7 · summary

Moving the catalyst buys a constant, near-fresh performance

  • Model: lumped gas balances per reactor; one mid-point activity per reactor from the coke balance.
  • CCR at 1050 kg/h: $a$ = 0.95 / 0.86 / 0.73 / 0.57, aromatics 0.582 every day.
  • The same beds held still pass below that within about two days.
  • Deactivation shows first as smaller temperature drops in R3 and R4.

17-8

Lecture 17-8

How is a coked catalyst made new again, every few days?

Four stepsLow oxygenBurn dutyPlatinum dispersion

Lecture 17-8

The regenerator is a second moving-bed reactor, run as a burner

  1. Four zones, four jobsburn, chlorinate, dry, reduce
  2. Why the oxygen is kept loweach mole per cent of O2 heats the gas by about 125 K
  3. Sizing the burnheat, gas flow and temperature rise from the coke rate
  4. Watching the regeneratorplatinum dispersion, screens and fines

Regenerator · click a zone

Burn the coke, redisperse the platinum, dry, then reduce

Click a zone of the regenerator

Coked catalyst enters at the top, falls through four zones in a few hours, and leaves ready for the reactors.

The whole regeneration takes only hours, so the catalyst can pass through it every few days for hundreds of cycles (Antos, Ch. 11).

The burn is the step that can destroy the catalyst it is meant to restore.

Low oxygen

Every mole per cent of oxygen burned heats the gas by about 125 K

$$\Delta T_{ad}=\frac{y_{O_2}\,(-\Delta H_{C})}{\bar c_p}=\frac{y_{O_2}\times393.5\ \text{kJ/mol}}{31\ \text{J/(mol K)}}$$
$y_{O_2}$
O2 mole fraction burned from the gas
–
$-\Delta H_C$
C + O2 → CO2, per mol O2
kJ/mol
$\bar c_p$
burn gas, mostly N2, near 750 K
J/(mol K)

Coke treated as carbon; its hydrogen adds a little more heat per mole of O2.

  • Burns start near 400 °C with 0.5–2 % O2; keep coke burn-off below about 565 °C (Antos, Ch. 11).
  • Inside a burning pellet it can be 110–170 K hotter than the gas.
  • Too hot: Pt sinters, and alumina changes phase above 850 °C.

Example 17.4 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 17.4Sizing the burn zone

Example 17.2: coke made $R_c$ = 51.5 kg/h.

All the coke made in the reformer of Example 17.2 is burned in the regenerator. Treat the coke as carbon. The burn gas enters at 480 °C with 0.8 mol% O2, and all the oxygen is consumed; its mean heat capacity is 31 J/(mol K).

(a) What heat does the burn release? (b) What burn-gas flow is needed? (c) What is the gas temperature rise? (d) What inlet O2 keeps the gas outlet at or below 560 °C?

Example 17.4 · solution

EXAMPLE 17.40.47 MW, 536 kmol/h of gas, +102 K: too hot; 0.63 % O2 is the limit

Previous slide but one$\Delta T_{ad}=\dfrac{y_{O_2}(-\Delta H_C)}{\bar c_p}$
(a) $\dot n_C=\dfrac{51.5}{12}=4.29$ kmol/h;  $\dot Q=4.29\times393.5=1689$ MJ/h $=0.47$ MW
one O2 per carbon
(b) $\dot n_{gas}=\dfrac{4.29}{0.008}=536$ kmol/h
all oxygen consumed
(c) $\Delta T=\dfrac{0.008\times393\,500}{31}=102$ K $\Rightarrow$ 582 °C
above the 565 °C guide
(d) $y_{O_2}\le\dfrac{80\times31}{393\,500}=0.0063$; gas flow rises to 680 kmol/h
trade O2 for gas recycle

Burn duty · try it

Less oxygen means a cooler burn but more gas to circulate

Example 17.4$\Delta T=\dfrac{y_{O_2}(-\Delta H_C)}{\bar c_p},\quad \dot n_{gas}=\dfrac{\dot n_C}{y_{O_2}}$
outlet (°C)–
gas (kmol/h)–
heat (MW)–

The outlet temperature depends on O2 and inlet only; the coke rate sets how much gas must flow. Burn capacity limits how low the reactor pressure can go.

A regenerator can run every day and still slowly damage the catalyst.

Platinum dispersion

Track platinum dispersion: it falls before the yields do

  • Efficiency = per cent rise in Pt dispersion, regenerated against spent catalyst.
  • Plugged screens starved air and chloride: dispersion fell to 30 % in a year.
  • Fines plug screens; elutriation at the top removes them (Antos, Ch. 11).

Section 17-8 · summary

The regenerator restores the catalyst only if its burn is gentle

  • Four zones: burn coke, oxychlorinate (Pt redispersion, Cl 1.0–1.1 wt%), dry, reduce in H2.
  • $\Delta T_{ad}\approx125$ K per mol% O2: keep O2 below about 1 %.
  • Coke rate sets heat and gas flow; burn capacity limits reactor severity.
  • Falling Pt dispersion is the early warning; keep screens clean and fines out.

Revamp path · click a step

Each revamp step lowers pressure and needs a bigger regenerator

–

–

Raseev, Table 13.17: investment rises from 9.5 to 35 M USD and the product value from 6.9 to 25.5 M USD/yr, so payback stays near 1.3–1.9 years.

Decision rule

Move the catalyst when the cycle at the best pressure is days, not months

  1. Find the pressure that maximizes yieldfor reforming, as low as the burn capacity allows
  2. Estimate the cycle at that pressure$C_{c,max}/r_c$ from pilot or licensor data
  3. Months: fixed bed. Weeks: cyclic. Days: moving beda day or less: fluidized
  4. Check the value against the hardwarehydrogen, yield, on-stream time against regenerator cost

Section 17-9 · summary

A CCR is worth it when low pressure pays more than the regenerator costs

  • SR: no extra hardware, declining yields. Cyclic: a swing reactor. CCR: a regenerator loop.
  • Extra yield of a CCR: more C5+, more and purer H2, constant all year.
  • Revamps step pressure from 12 to 7 to 3.5 bar, with growing regenerators.
  • Cycle at the best pressure in days: move the catalyst.

Problem 17.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 17.1A dehydrogenation catalyst loop

A propane dehydrogenation unit with radial moving-bed reactors processes 60 t/h of propane at 40 % conversion per pass. The reactors hold 50 t of catalyst, and the catalyst makes one pass through the reactors every 7 days. Spent catalyst leaves with 3.0 wt% coke; regenerated catalyst returns with 0.1 wt% coke.

(a) Find the catalyst circulation rate. (b) Find the coke made, in kg/h. (c) Express it per tonne of propane converted. (d) If the loop is shortened to 5 days at the same coke make, what coke leaves the last reactor?

Propane feed60 t/h
Conversion per pass40 %
Catalyst in reactors $W$50 t
Loop time7 d
$C_{c,out}$, $C_{c,in}$3.0 wt%, 0.1 wt%

Problem 17.1 · solution

PROBLEM 17.1298 kg/h of catalyst, 8.6 kg/h of coke, 0.36 kg per tonne converted

Coke balance, Lecture 17-6$F_s\big(C_{c,out}-C_{c,in}\big)=R_c,\qquad \tau_s=\dfrac{W}{F_s}$
(a) $F_s=\dfrac{50\,000}{7\times24}=298$ kg/h
loop time gives circulation
(b) $R_c=298\times(0.030-0.001)=8.63$ kg/h   (c) $\dfrac{8.63}{0.40\times60}=0.36$ kg/t
24 t/h propane converted
(d) $F_s=\dfrac{50\,000}{120}=417$ kg/h;  $C_{c,out}=0.001+\dfrac{8.63}{417}=2.17$ wt%
faster loop, less coke

Problem 17.1 · try it

Fix the coke make; the loop time sets the coke on the spent catalyst

Coke balance$C_{c,out}=C_{c,in}+\dfrac{R_c\,\tau_s}{W}$
$C_{c,out}$ at 7 d (wt%)–
loop for 3 wt% (d)–

Spent coke rises linearly with loop time: halving the loop halves the coke the catalyst carries.

Problem 17.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 17.2How much more gas?

A refiner wants to raise the gas flow through the last reactor of a CCR reformer by 30 %. The radial bed has $r_i$ = 0.5 m, $r_o$ = 1.4 m, $H$ = 7 m and bulk density 650 kg/m³; its measured pressure drop today is 9 kPa. Take the catalyst–screen friction coefficient as 0.3 and the drag as $F_d\approx\Delta P\cdot2\pi r_mH$ with $r_m=(r_i+r_o)/2$. In this regime $\Delta P\propto Q^{1.65}$.

(a) Is the bed safe from pinning today? (b) After the 30 % increase? (c) What is the largest flow increase before pinning?

$r_i$, $r_o$, $H$0.5, 1.4, 7 m
$\rho_b$650 kg/m³
$\Delta P$ today9 kPa
$\mu_w$0.3
$\Delta P\propto Q^{n}$$n$ = 1.65

Problem 17.2 · solution

PROBLEM 17.2$\Pi$ = 0.47 today, 0.73 after the revamp; pinning at about +58 %

Pinning ratio, Lecture 17-5$\Pi=\dfrac{\mu_w F_d}{\rho_b g V_{bed}},\qquad F_d\approx\Delta P\cdot2\pi r_mH$
$V_{bed}=\pi(1.4^2-0.5^2)\times7=37.6$ m³;  weight $=650\times9.81\times37.6=2.40\times10^5$ N
bed weight
(a) $F_d=9000\times2\pi\times0.95\times7=3.76\times10^5$ N;  $\Pi=\dfrac{0.3\times3.76\times10^5}{2.40\times10^5}=0.47$
safe today
(b) $\Pi=0.47\times1.3^{1.65}=0.73$   (c) $Q_{max}/Q=(1/0.47)^{1/1.65}=1.58$
$\Pi\propto\Delta P\propto Q^{1.65}$

The mean-radius drag overestimates the exact integral by about 13 %, so the margin is conservative.

Problem 17.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 17.3The regenerator trips

Example 17.3: mid-point coke 0.345, 1.08, 2.30, 4.02 wt%; $r_c=5.7\times10^{-4}$ h−1; $a=e^{-13.9C_c}$.

In the reformer of Example 17.3 the regenerator trips. Catalyst circulation stops, but naphtha keeps flowing at the same conditions, so every reactor now behaves as a fixed bed.

(a) What are the activities at the mid-points of R1 and R4 after 24 hours? (b) How many hours until the catalyst at the mid-point of R4 reaches 7 wt% coke, the upper limit for spent catalyst quoted by Antos (Ch. 11)?

Problem 17.3 · solution

PROBLEM 17.3After a day R4 is at a = 0.47; it reaches 7 wt% in about 52 h

Fixed bed, Lecture 17-6$C_c(t)=C_{c,0}+r_c\,t,\qquad a=e^{-\alpha C_c}$
24 h adds $5.7\times10^{-4}\times24=0.0137$ = 1.37 wt% to every reactor
same $r_c$ everywhere
(a) R1: $e^{-13.9\times0.0172}=0.79$ (was 0.95);  R4: $e^{-13.9\times0.0539}=0.47$ (was 0.57)
mid-point coke plus 1.37 wt%
(b) $t=\dfrac{0.070-0.0402}{5.7\times10^{-4}}=52$ h
about two days of margin

In one day R1 loses more activity than in its whole normal pass.

Lecture 17

Key Takeaways

1

Choose a moving bed when the catalyst lives days to weeks at the best operating pressure.

2

Write the balances with age = position: $F_s(C_{c,out}-C_{c,in})=r_cW$ sets the circulation.

3

Use radial cross-flow beds for low pressure drop, and keep $\Pi=\mu_wF_d/(\rho_bgV_{bed})$ below 1.

4

Burn coke with under 1 % O2: each mol% heats the gas by about 125 K.

5

Judge a CCR by constant, near-fresh yields and extra hydrogen against regenerator cost.
